proposed.text: An architect's moral rights under RA 8293 include attribution and objection to prejudicial distortion. Which scenario most clearly tests a moral-rights violation?

options.text: A building owner performs routine maintenance by replacing worn exterior wall finishes with matching materials
A building owner adds interior building services without changing the public attribution or distinctive design expression
A building owner removes the architect's attribution from public use of the work and presents the design without credit
A building owner replaces windows while maintaining the original mullion pattern and design character

rationale.a: Routine like-for-like maintenance does not by itself show lack of attribution or prejudicial distortion.
rationale.b: Interior services may be a functional change; more facts are needed before treating it as a Section 193 violation.
rationale.d: Maintaining the original design character weakens, rather than proves, an integrity claim.
rationale.correct: RA 8293 Section 193 gives the author the right to require attribution as far as practicable and to object to prejudicial distortion or mutilation. Removing the architect's attribution from public use of the work directly tests attribution. Routine maintenance or functional upgrades require separate facts before they become prejudicial distortion.
rationale.takeaway: Moral-rights questions usually turn on attribution or prejudicial distortion, not ordinary maintenance.
